item.title: Bombardier to buy Mitsubishi aerospace plant near Pearson airport
item.description: Bombardier Inc. says it will buy Mitsubishi’s main Canadian aerospace factory, bringing in-house an operation that was previously outsourced.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — Bombardier Inc. says it will buy Mitsubishi’s main Canadian aerospace factory, bringing in-house an operation that was previously outsourced. The Montreal-based business jet maker says the purchase of MHI Canada Aerospace Inc. facilities in Mississauga, Ont., will see some 750 Mitsubishi employees join Bombardier’s roughly 18,000-person workforce. The deal also means MHI’s 270,000 square-foot plant that handles wing assembly, fuselage and flight control installations for some Bombardier planes will now fall under that company’s umbrella. David Murray, executive vice-president of manufacturing, says the agreement marks a key step in the company’s long-term growth strategy as demand remains on the upswing. Bombardier did not specify a purchase amount for the factory, which sits on the outskirts of Toronto’s Pearson airport. The announcement comes a month after CEO Éric Martel said the manufacturer was starting to eye acquisitions in aircraft services and defence, as the appetite for its business jets continues to grow and a once-towering debt load comes back to earth. The deal, which is subject to regulatory approvals, is expected to close later this year. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1 2026

item.title: ‘Do you know how much new signs cost?’: U.S. businesses vow to keep ‘Ontario’ in names
item.description: Business owners in upstate New York say they have no plans to drop ‘Ontario’ from their names following Trump’s ‘Lake America’ executive order.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Otis
item.content:encoded: Business owners in upstate New York say they have no plans to drop “Ontario” from their names following Trump’s “Lake America” executive order. “Our business was named after Lake Ontario, and most of our equipment, attractions, and décor were designed with the lake, water, and nautical themes in mind,” Ontario Play & Café owner Pouya Seifzadeh told CTVNews.ca in an email Monday. “When the renaming was announced, we had a great laugh about unexpectedly finding ourselves in the middle of the story.” Amid trade tensions with Canada, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to rename the lake, which has been known as Lake Ontario for more than four centuries. The switch to “Lake America” has been met with firm condemnation from Canadians as well as Trump’s opponents in the U.S. The change also prompted a cheeky Instagram post from Seifzadeh’s indoor playground and café, which is located in Rochester, N.Y., the largest American city on the lake. “POV: You named your entire business after Lake Ontario… and then woke up today,” Ontario Play & Café posted on Friday. “Do you know how much new signs cost?” After more than a decade in business, thousands of children have celebrated their birthdays or frolicked at Ontario Play & Café. With a pirate ship play structure, water station and sand table, the 1,300-square-metre indoor playground leans heavily into its nautical theme. The “Ontario” name is also featured on everything from staff T-shirts to plastic cups. “The name has become part of our identity and our relationship with local families,” Seifzadeh, a dual Canada-U.S. citizen, explained. “Therefore, our official position regarding our own business is simple: Ontario Play & Café is not changing its name.” ‘We’re always going to carry Lake Ontario merchandise’ Amanda Miller is the owner of both the Lake Ontario Gift Shop and Lake Ontario Realty in New York’s Jefferson County, which sits at the eastern end of the lake. Citing brand recognition and associated costs, Miller says she has no intention to change the names of her businesses – but she isn’t against the idea of stocking “Lake America” souvenirs at her gift shop in the future “We’re going to prepare for what consumers are requesting,” Miller told CTVNews.ca by phone on Tuesday. “But at the end of the day, we’re always going to carry Lake Ontario merchandise.”Located near the water in Rochester, the Lake Ontario Press screen printing shop also has no plans to change its name. “The name change is just a silly waste of time,” owner Matt Saxon told CTVNews.ca by email on Monday. “My business will remain Lake Ontario Press.” The business prominently sells “Lake Ontario” t-shirts and posters on its website. “I will not be calling it anything other than Lake Ontario,” Saxon added. “We cannot move on from this quick enough.” ‘A clear distraction’ Rochester’s city council has also flatly rejected the “Lake America” name. In a proclamation released on Friday, the nine-member council unanimously slammed the name change as being as “childish as it is futile” and vowed to continue referring to “Lake Ontario” in all official capacities. “This desperate and flaccid stunt by the President is a clear distraction from the issues that matter most to U.S. voters: the failing economy, housing, affordability and, lest we forget, President Trump’s unwanted and unwarranted war with Iran,” the proclamation read. “No serious person from the Native Tribes or U.S. and Canadian cities which share the Lake will ever call Lake Ontario ‘Lake America.’” The proclamation also criticized the “futile trade conflict with Canada – among our nation’s most important and dependable allies.” Following the “Lake America” name change, Seifzadeh said he remains focused on the “fun and humour” of the situation, joking that “nobody had consulted us.” “We will leave the politics, the reasons behind the decision, and predictions about whether the new name will stick to others,” Seifzadeh added. “We will continue concentrating on what we do best, which is creating a fun and enjoyable place for children and families.”

item.title: Government borrowing costs rise anew, adding to pressure on global policymakers
item.description: A selloff in global bond markets deepened, reflecting investor angst over inflation and government debt levels that stand to inflict fresh pain on consumers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: TOKYO/LONDON/SINGAPORE — A selloff in global bond markets deepened on Tuesday, reflecting investor angst over inflation and government debt levels that stand to inflict fresh pain on consumers and businesses. Japan’s 10-year yield hit 3 per cent for the first time since 1996 as the rout hit bond prices, driving up yields, in major economies around the globe. Yields hit their highest in 15 years in Germany and their highest since 2008 in the UK. In the U.S., the 10-year yield US10YT=RR rose three basis points to 4.788 per cent, putting it in range of its highest level since 2023. Some of the world’s leading economies, notably the U.S., have sharply increased their debt loads in recent years through deficit spending, with the U.S. debt hitting US$40 trillion - a shift investors warn is likely structural rather than episodic and will be difficult to remedy without tough choices at the national level. Meanwhile wars from Russia-Ukraine to the Middle East have sent oil and gas prices higher, adding to pressure on interest rates and the cost of living. “This is likely primarily a U.S.-specific story, though global currents are amplifying it,” said David Krakauer, vice president of portfolio management at Mercer Advisors. “The core drivers are largely domestic: deficit spending, the cost of servicing a rising debt load, and shifting Treasury auction dynamics,” in which price-sensitive buyers such as hedge funds and other private firms have in part supplanted price-insensitive official buyers such as central banks. A deluge of bond sales from big tech companies aggressively raising money to fund the AI boom is adding to the pressure on bonds. Governments are jittery. The U.S. Treasury stepped into markets last month in a bid to cap a rise in borrowing costs, which can spill over to higher loan rates for everything from household mortgages to business loans. Yields on 30-year Treasuries US30YT=RR are close to the highest in 19 years. “Many developed markets have seen their long-term funding costs rise, as borrowing needs from both the public and private sectors have increased,” HSBC chief Asia economist Frederic Neumann said. Inflation, fiscal worries The scale of the global shift is underscored by the rise in 10-year Japanese government bond yields to 3 per cent for the first time in 30 years, something seen as practically unthinkable until recently after over a decade of massive central bank debt purchases kept rates artificially low. “The stalemate in the Middle East risks pushing energy prices higher. ... Meanwhile, few actions have been taken to consolidate fiscal deficits in both economies,” Tai Hui, APAC chief market strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said of the move in U.S. and Japanese yields. Brent crude rose nearly 2 per cent to over US$92 a barrel LCOc1 on Tuesday and European natural gas prices were at their highest since March, after Monday saw the first exchange of direct attacks between the U.S. and Iran in a month. End of era? Definitely For Japan in particular, higher yields increase the cost of servicing the developed world’s biggest debt pile at a time when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is planning aggressive investment. U.S. 10-year Treasury yields US10YT=RR pushed to the highest since January 2025 at 4.798 per cent, while the 30-year yield was at 5.27 per cent just 6 basis points shy of levels before August’s intervention. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says that worries about rising debt and yields overlook the strength of the U.S. economy. Germany’s 10-year yield was at 3.35 per cent, its highest since 2011, DE10YT=RR, as data showed euro zone inflation rose above 3 per cent in August, cementing bets on a September European Central Bank rate rise, while Britain’s 10-year gilt yield GB10YT=RR rose to 5.25 per cent, its highest since 2008. British and euro zone yields hit fresh over-10-year highs as the Middle East crisis stoked price pressures globally, driving market bets that central banks will raise interest rates soon. Real yields a driver Analysts noted some different forces at play as global borrowing costs rise. “In Europe and the UK it is more because of heightened inflation expectations, while in the U.S. the upticks in long-end yields are still more driven by higher real yields, although inflation expectations have been creeping up too,” said Frances Cheung, OCBC’s head of FX and rates strategy. Real yields are the returns that a bond investor demands above inflation, an indicator of true borrowing costs for governments and companies, and can be affected by several factors, including long-run economic growth. Bessent also shrugged off worries about the bond market in an interview with Reuters on Sunday, saying the effect of higher energy prices would fade. Michiel Tukker, senior rates analyst at ING, said economic growth combined with higher deficits and bond sales are pushing up real yields. “There’s no easy turnaround ... and if you ask who will take the other side of this trade (i.e. betting yields will fall), that’s difficult to see,” he said. And the global story can become self-reinforcing, since higher yields in one market can push them up elsewhere. Australian 10-year yields AU10YT=RR notched their sharpest rise in five months on Tuesday, in part due to fears higher JGB yields would mean fewer Japanese buyers of Australian debt. Further Japanese yield rises could drive a gradual re-allocation into Japanese assets, said TD Securities senior rates strategist Prashant Newnaha. “It’s a genuine regime change. JGBs were the anchor for global fixed income for a long time,” he said. “Now it has flipped.” --- Reporting by Kevin Buckland in Tokyo, Rae Wee in Singapore, Alun John in London and Laura Matthews in New York; Editing by Susan Fenton, Colin Barr and Daniel Wallis

item.title: Bruce Campbell’s Top Picks for Sept. 1, 2026
item.description: Second-quarter earnings were exceptionally strong, with corporate profits growing at one of the fastest rates of the past two decades. Although valuations remain a frequent concern, valuation alone ...
item.content:encoded:
Bruce Campbell, President & Portfolio Manager, StoneCastle Investment Management Focus: Canadian stocks

Top Picks: K92 Mining , TMX Group , Amerigo Resources MARKET OUTLOOK: Investors have been forced to navigate an extraordinary amount of macro noise, from tariffs and geopolitical conflict to volatile commodity prices, inflation, U.S. Federal Reserve policy and changing liquidity conditions. That uncertainty along with slowing economic momentum in July helped trigger one of the most significant momentum rotations we have seen in the past 25 years. However, as we head into the fall, the underlying environment appears to be stabilizing. Second-quarter earnings were exceptionally strong, with corporate profits growing at one of the fastest rates of the past two decades. Although valuations remain a frequent concern, valuation alone rarely ends a bull market. If earnings continue to grow and economic conditions stay steady, today’s valuations can be supported. We are currently positioned on offense. All the top-down indicators we follow: including economic growth, market breadth, trend and momentum, remain positive. One of our research partners, which models changes in growth and inflation, expects favourable market conditions through September and into the fourth quarter of 2026. Its models suggest the environment could become more challenging between February and May 2027, but we are not positioning for that prematurely. For now, we continue to focus on companies demonstrating accelerating revenue and earnings growth where the market has not yet fully recognized the opportunity. Market-moving news, fast:  Get the BNN Bloomberg App now Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at  bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters TOP PICKS: Bruce Campbell's Top Picks: K92 Mining, TMX Group & Amerigo Resources Bruce Campbell, president & portfolio manager at StoneCastle Investment Management, shares his top stock picks to watch in the market.

K92 Mining (KNT TSX) Operates a high-grade, low-cost gold mine in Papua New Guinea and is advancing a fully funded expansion that is currently on schedule and on budget. The company is ramping up toward its longer-term objective of approximately 500,000 ounces of annual production yet continues to trade at a discount to many comparable gold producers. After a period of consolidation, gold prices appear to be accelerating again, supported by continued central-bank purchases and renewed demand from gold ETFs. That combination of rising production and stronger gold prices could translate into significant earnings and cash-flow growth for K92. TMX Group (X TSX) Operates Canada’s leading capital-markets exchanges but is increasingly becoming a diversified global financial-infrastructure and data company. Through acquisitions and organic expansion, TMX has deliberately increased its international exposure and grown its base of recurring revenue, making the business less dependent on Canadian trading and financing activity. The company also generates strong cash flow, supporting continued investment and a growing dividend. Earlier concerns that artificial intelligence, blockchain and decentralized finance could disrupt traditional exchanges have moderated, allowing investors to focus again on TMX’s expanding global footprint and consistent growth. Amerigo Resources (ARG TSX) Is best understood as a “copper factory.” Rather than exploring for or developing mines, Amerigo processes tailings from Codelco’s El Teniente operation in Chile, the world’s largest underground copper mine. This makes the company a strong proxy for copper prices while avoiding much of the exploration and mine-development risk associated with traditional producers. Amerigo returns capital to shareholders through three channels: a regular dividend, performance-based dividends tied to cash flow, and share buybacks. As copper prices rise, stronger cash flow can support all three while increasing the underlying value of the business.
